subject_line: Cataplexy and the old myth in Daphne
email_body:
Dear Will,

Daphne sets the Apollo and Daphne myth in San Francisco in 2011, amid the protests, and gives its heroine cataplexy, so that strong emotion leaves her literally unable to move. In your Rumpus conversation you made clear the condition is real, not a metaphor invented for the myth. I would like to ask how you balanced medical accuracy against the pull of the old story, and whether teaching fiction at Royal Holloway has changed how you think about retelling myths.

subject_line: Alice B. Toklas's horn and the reluctant investigator
email_body:
Dear Prudence,

Bone Horn sends a newly registered private investigator after proof that Alice B. Toklas had a horn growing from her forehead, a rumour Picasso repeated, and the narrator takes the case mostly for the money. I would like to ask how a stray piece of modernist gossip turned into a novel about queerness and grief, and how it felt to move into detective fiction after your poetry and the critical work on queer flippancy. It seems that flippancy might be doing serious work here too.

subject_line: Writing beside the camera in Film Poems
email_body:
Dear Redell,

Film Poems gathers sequences such as Bucolic Picnic, Lost Pool and SPRIGS & spots, each first written alongside a film you made or remade, so the page carries traces of a screen it no longer has. I would like to ask what happens to those poems once they are separated from their films, and whether you now write differently knowing a text might live on paper alone. I would also like to hear how this links to The Minimaus Poems, your answer to Olson.

subject_line: Writing Dudley's Brexit vote in The Cut
email_body:
Dear Anthony,

The Cut was written as part of Peirene's Peirene Now! series of fiction responding to current events, and you set it in Dudley, your hometown, which voted decisively to leave the EU. Reviewers describe a relationship built on misunderstanding, intolerance and guilt. I would like to ask what it was like to write about your own town on a commission tied to a national moment, and how the book reads to you now, years after the referendum, from UWE Bristol.

book_title: Everybody Needs Beauty: In Search of the Nature Cure
subject_line: From Lourdes to a laboratory forest in Everybody Needs Beauty
email_body:
Dear Samantha,

Everybody Needs Beauty takes the nature cure seriously while questioning how the wellness industry sells it, and the route is memorable: the waters of Lourdes, a turn-of-the-century wilderness retreat in Maine, a forest bathing centre in Finland, and a laboratory that simulates nature indoors. I would like to ask which of those places most unsettled your own assumptions, and how you hold together real care for the healing power of the natural world with scepticism about its commercial packaging.

subject_line: Forty-eight films for a secular Book of Hours
email_body:
Dear Lucy,

The Book of Hours reimagines the medieval devotional book as a calendar of forty-eight poetry films, one for each of four times of day across the twelve months, each made with a different filmmaker, with the poems also published by Burning Eye Books. You have described it as secular yet meditative. I would like to ask what working with so many collaborators taught you about letting a poem change in someone else's hands, and how the spoken word stage shaped the project.

book_title: Pseudonymous HarperCollins novels (retellings of Clarissa and The Tenant of Wildfell Hall)
subject_line: Clarissa and Wildfell Hall as psychological suspense
email_body:
Dear Tracy,

Your Bath Spa profile mentions that one of your novels retells Samuel Richardson's Clarissa and another Anne Brontë's The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, and that readers tend to call them literary thrillers or psychological suspense. I find that pairing fascinating: two classic novels about women trapped by men, reread through the machinery of suspense. I would like to ask what those older books gave you that a wholly invented plot could not, and how writing under a pseudonym sits alongside your work as a critic.

subject_line: Under the dome in Dark Parties, and after
email_body:
Dear Sara,

Dark Parties, your first young adult novel, follows a girl born inside a domed country and won the SCBWI Crystal Kite Award for Europe; Half Lives then split its story between teens before and after an apocalypse. You also commission series fiction at Working Partners and co-founded Undiscovered Voices. I would like to ask how moving between your own dystopias, younger series like Magic Trix and helping unpublished writers find their way has shaped what you teach on Goldsmiths' children's and teen writing courses.

subject_line: The unnamed country in Study for Obedience
email_body:
Dear Sarah,

Study for Obedience sends its unnamed narrator to a remote part of an unnamed northern country to keep house for her older brother after his marriage ends, and she soon feels the community's hostility gathering around her. You told The Skinny the setting is somewhere in Eastern Europe yet never specified. I would like to ask why withholding the place mattered so much to the book, and whether writing from near Ullapool, itself on an edge, fed that sense of displacement.

subject_line: Rab Dillon's guitar, from Glasgow to Brighton
email_body:
Dear Liam,

The Busker follows Rab Dillon, a young Glasgow protest singer whose career collapses and leaves him homeless in Brighton, with the Occupy movement and the music industry running through the book. Since then have come Man at Sea and The Sleepless, and a move to Strathclyde. I would like to ask how your sense of political fiction has changed between So It Is, with its women of the Troubles, and the more recent novels, and what Rab taught you about writing music on the page.

subject_line: The rainy season of 1995 in And After Many Days
email_body:
Dear Jowhor,

And After Many Days begins with seventeen-year-old Paul Utu going missing in Port Harcourt during the rainy season of 1995, and the family's search slowly opens up secrets they had kept from one another. The novel won the Etisalat Prize, the first time a Nigerian took it. I would like to ask how you built a whole family's history around an absence, and how teaching in Aberystwyth, so far from Port Harcourt, affects the way you return to that city on the page.

Dear Daniele,

ORAKL takes a loose translation of all of Georg Trakl's poems and then reorders the lines alphabetically by their first words, which turns a translator's devotion into something closer to a new poem. It sits beside your more conventional work on Trakl and your Robert Walser translations, Oppressive Light and the Dramolettes. I would like to ask what the alphabet revealed in Trakl that faithful translation could not, and how moving between the two modes has shaped your own poetry.

subject_line: Victor Lennon and Fr Benedict in Madden
email_body:
Dear Darran,

After the Lockout brings Victor Lennon, a Marxist veteran of the 1913 Lockout and the Easter Rising, home to the Armagh village of Madden in late 1917, and lets his struggle with the parish priest, Fr Stanislaus Benedict, unfold through both men's perspectives. I would like to ask why you chose to give the priest an equal voice rather than keeping the story with Victor, and how writing about your own county shaped the book.

subject_line: Jamie's perpetual motion machine and the currach
email_body:
Dear Elaine,

How to Build a Boat gives thirteen-year-old Jamie O'Neill two missions, building a perpetual motion machine and finding a way to connect with the mother who died when he was born, and lets that project draw in his teachers, Tess and Tadhg. One reader called it an ode to teachers, and the currach chapter seems central. I would like to ask how you went about writing practical craft, boat-building itself, into a novel about grief, and how your poetry shaped Jamie's voice.
